rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: \(\left(\sqrt{3} + 2\right)^2 + \left(\sqrt{3} - 2\right)^2\) is a/an
rows.solution:
\((\sqrt{3} + 2)^2 + (\sqrt{3} - 2)^2 = (7 + 4\sqrt{3}) + (7 - 4\sqrt{3}) = 14\).

14 is a positive rational number, which is option (A) positive rational number.

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Let \(x = a^2 b^3 c^n\) and \(y = a^3 b^m c^2\), where a, b, c are prime numbers. If LCM of x and y is \(a^3 b^4 c^3\), then the value of \(m + n\) is
rows.solution:
The LCM takes the highest power of each prime.

For b: the higher of \(b^3\) and \(b^m\) is \(b^4\), so \(m = 4\). For c: the higher of \(c^n\) and \(c^2\) is \(c^3\), so \(n = 3\).

\(m + n = 7\), which is option (B) \(7\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: For any prime number p, if p divides \(a^2\), where a is any real number then p also divides
rows.solution:
The theorem: if a prime p divides \(a^2\), then p divides a (for a positive integer a). The stem's "any real number" should read "positive integer"; divisibility is defined only for integers.

This is option (A) \(a\).

rows.stem: Which of the following equations is a quadratic equation ?
rows.solution:
Expand each and see what degree is left:

\(x^2 + 1 = x^2 - 2x + 1\) gives \(2x = 0\), which is linear.

\((x + \sqrt{x})^2 = 2x\sqrt{x}\) gives \(x^2 + 2x\sqrt{x} + x = 2x\sqrt{x}\), that is \(x^2 + x = 0\), which is quadratic.

\(x^3 + 3x^2 = x^3 + 3x^2 + 3x + 1\) gives \(3x + 1 = 0\), which is linear.

\(x^2 - 1 = x^2 + 2x + 1\) gives \(2x + 2 = 0\), which is linear.

This is option (B) \((x + \sqrt{x})^2 = 2x\sqrt{x}\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: If \(x^2 + bx + b = 0\) has two real and distinct roots, then the value of b can be
rows.solution:
Two real and distinct roots need \(b^2 - 4b > 0\), that is \(b(b - 4) > 0\), so \(b < 0\) or \(b > 4\).

Of the choices only \(-3\) qualifies (0 and 4 give equal roots, and 3 gives no real roots). This is option (D) \(-3\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: In the figure given below, points P, Q, R divides the line segment AB in four equal parts. The point Q divides PB in the ratio
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the order of the points along the segment (A, P, Q, R, B) is shown only in the drawing, and the ratio in which Q divides PB depends on it. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
A, P, Q, R, B divide AB into four equal parts, so \(PQ\) is one part and \(QB\) is two parts.

\(PQ : QB = 1 : 2\), which is option (C) 1 : 2.

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: A bag contains red balls and black balls in the ratio 3 : 7. A ball is drawn at random. The probability that ball so drawn is black in colour, is
rows.solution:
Red and black are in the ratio \(3 : 7\), so 7 of every 10 balls are black.

\(P(\text{black}) = \dfrac{7}{10} = 0.7\), which is option (C) \(0.7\).

rows.stem: Which of the following statements is false ?

options.label: A
options.text: Two right triangles are always similar.

options.label: C
options.text: Two equilateral triangles are always similar.

rows.solution:
Squares, equilateral triangles and circles each have one shape, so any two of a kind are similar. Two right triangles share only the right angle: their other angles can differ (a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle and a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle), so they need not be similar.

The false statement is option (A) Two right triangles are always similar.

rows.stem: In the adjoining figure, ABCD is a trapezium in which \(XY \parallel AB \parallel CD\). If \(AX = \dfrac{2}{3} AD\), then \(CY : YB =\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - trapezium ABCD (AB the lower base, DC the upper) with X on AD and Y on BC; the stem states the data. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
\(AX = \dfrac{2}{3}AD\), so \(XD = \dfrac{1}{3}AD\) and \(DX : XA = 1 : 2\).

Three parallel lines (CD, XY, AB) cut the two transversals in the same ratio, so \(CY : YB = DX : XA = 1 : 2\).

This is option (D) 1 : 2.

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: Which of the following statements is false ?

options.label: A
options.text: Infinite number of tangents can be drawn to a circle.

options.label: B
options.text: Infinite number of tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point outside the circle.

options.label: C
options.text: Infinite number of secants can be drawn to a circle from a point outside the circle.

options.label: D
options.text: Angle between tangent and diameter at point of contact is \(90^\circ\).

rows.solution:
From a point outside a circle exactly two tangents can be drawn, not infinitely many. The other statements are true.

The false statement is option (B) Infinite number of tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point outside the circle.

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the adjoining figure, PA and PB are tangents to a circle with centre O. The measure of angle APB is
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the only datum, the reflex angle AOB of 210 degrees, is given only in the drawing. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The reflex angle AOB is \(210^\circ\), so \(\angle AOB = 360^\circ - 210^\circ = 150^\circ\).

\(OA \perp PA\) and \(OB \perp PB\), so in quadrilateral OAPB, \(\angle APB = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ\).

This is option (D) \(30^\circ\).

rows.stem: \(\dfrac{1 - \tan^2 30^\circ}{1 + \tan^2 30^\circ}\) is equal to
rows.solution:
\(\tan^2 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{1 - \frac{1}{3}}{1 + \frac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{2/3}{4/3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\), which is option (B) \(\cos 60^\circ\).

rows.stem: An observer 1.8 m tall stands away from a chimney at a distance of 38.2 m along the ground. The angle of elevation of top of chimney from the eyes of observer is \(45^\circ\). The height of chimney above the ground is
rows.solution:
At \(45^\circ\) the height of the chimney above the observer's eyes equals the horizontal distance, 38.2 m.

Height above the ground \(= 38.2 + 1.8 = 40\) m, which is option (C) 40 m.

rows.stem: In the adjoining figure, the sum of radii of two concentric circles is 16 cm. The length of chord AB which touches the inner circle at P is 16 cm. The difference of the radii of the given circles is
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - two concentric circles with centre O and the chord AB of the outer circle touching the inner circle at P; the stem states every value. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
Let the radii be R and r. The chord AB touches the inner circle at P, so \(OP = r\), \(OP \perp AB\), and \(AP = \dfrac{16}{2} = 8\) cm.

In right triangle OPA: \(R^2 - r^2 = 8^2 = 64\), so \((R - r)(R + r) = 64\) and \(R - r = \dfrac{64}{16} = 4\) cm.

This is option (B) 4 cm.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A cone of height 12 cm and slant height 13 cm is surmounted on a hemisphere having radius equal to that of cone. The entire height of the solid is
rows.solution:
Radius of the cone \(= \sqrt{13^2 - 12^2} = 5\) cm, which is also the radius of the hemisphere.

Total height \(= 12 + 5 = 17\) cm, which is option (A) 17 cm.

rows.stem: If x median + y mean = z mode; is the empirical relationship between mean, median and mode, then the value of \(x + y + z\) is
rows.solution:
The empirical relation is \(3\,\)Median \(- 2\,\)Mean \(=\) Mode, so \(x = 3\), \(y = -2\) and \(z = 1\).

\(x + y + z = 3 - 2 + 1 = 2\), which is option (C) \(2\).

rows.stem:
Following data shows the marks obtained by 100 students in a class test :

| **Marks obtained** | 20 | 29 | 28 | 33 | 42 | 38 | 43 | 25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Number of students** | 6 | 28 | 24 | 15 | 2 | 4 | 1 | 20 |

The median will be the average of which two observations ?
rows.solution:
Arrange the marks in order with cumulative frequencies:

| Marks | 20 | 25 | 28 | 29 | 33 | 38 | 42 | 43 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Students | 6 | 20 | 24 | 28 | 15 | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| Cumulative | 6 | 26 | 50 | 78 | 93 | 97 | 99 | 100 |

With 100 observations the median is the average of the 50th and 51st. The 50th is 28 and the 51st is 29.

This is option (C) 28 and 29.

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: The probability of getting a composite number greater than 3 on throwing a die is
rows.solution:
The composite numbers on a die are 4 and 6, and both are greater than 3.

\(P = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** For an acute angle \(\theta\), \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5} \Rightarrow \cos\theta = -\dfrac{4}{5}\).

**Reason (R) :** For any value of \(\theta\), \((0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ)\) \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\).
rows.context: Directions : In Question Numbers 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the correct option from following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For an acute angle \(\cos\theta > 0\), so \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}\) gives \(\cos\theta = +\dfrac{4}{5}\), not \(-\dfrac{4}{5}\). The Assertion is false.

\(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) holds for every \(\theta\), so the Reason is true.

The Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** For an A.P., 3,6,9, …, 198, \(10^{\text{th}}\) term from the end is 168.

**Reason (R) :** If ‘a’ and ‘\(l\)’ are the first term and last term of an A.P. with common difference ‘d’, then \(n^{\text{th}}\) term from the end of the given A.P. is \(l - (n - 1)d\).
rows.context: Directions : In Question Numbers 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the correct option from following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
From the end, the AP is 198, 195, 192, ..., with common difference \(-3\). The 10th term from the end is \(198 - 9 \times 3 = 171\), not 168. The Assertion is false.

The nth term from the end is \(l - (n - 1)d\), so the Reason is true.

The Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: The cost of 2 kg apples and 1 kg of grapes on a day was found to be ₹ 320. The cost of 4 kg apples and 2 kg grapes was found to be ₹ 600. If cost of 1 kg of apples and 1 kg of grapes is ₹ x and ₹ y respectively, represent the given situation algebraically as a system of equations and check whether the system so obtained is consistent or not.
rows.solution:
\(2x + y = 320\) and \(4x + 2y = 600\).

\(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{320}{600} = \dfrac{8}{15}\).

\(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), so the lines are parallel and the system is inconsistent (no solution).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem:
Solve for x and y :

\(\sqrt{2}\,x + \sqrt{3}\,y = 5\) and

\(\sqrt{3}\,x - \sqrt{8}\,y = -\sqrt{6}\)
rows.solution:
Multiply the first equation by \(\sqrt{3}\): \(\sqrt{6}\,x + 3y = 5\sqrt{3}\) ... (1)

Multiply the second by \(\sqrt{2}\): \(\sqrt{6}\,x - 4y = -2\sqrt{3}\) ... (2)

Subtracting (2) from (1): \(7y = 7\sqrt{3}\), so \(y = \sqrt{3}\).

Then \(\sqrt{2}\,x + 3 = 5\), so \(\sqrt{2}\,x = 2\) and \(x = \sqrt{2}\).

\(x = \sqrt{2}\), \(y = \sqrt{3}\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: The coordinates of the end points of the line segment AB are \(A(-2, -2)\) and \(B(2, -4)\). P is the point on AB such that \(BP = \dfrac{4}{7} AB\). Find the coordinates of point P.
rows.solution:
\(BP = \dfrac{4}{7}AB\), so \(AP = \dfrac{3}{7}AB\) and P divides AB in the ratio \(AP : PB = 3 : 4\).

\(x = \dfrac{3 \times 2 + 4 \times (-2)}{3 + 4} = -\dfrac{2}{7}\), \(y = \dfrac{3 \times (-4) + 4 \times (-2)}{3 + 4} = -\dfrac{20}{7}\).

\(P = \left(-\dfrac{2}{7}, -\dfrac{20}{7}\right)\).

rows.stem: It is given that \(\sin(A - B) = \sin A \cos B - \cos A \sin B\). Use it to find the value of \(\sin 15^\circ\).
rows.solution:
\(\sin 15^\circ = \sin(45^\circ - 30^\circ) = \sin 45^\circ \cos 30^\circ - \cos 45^\circ \sin 30^\circ\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2\sqrt{2}}\), or \(\dfrac{\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}}{4}\).

rows.stem: If \(\sin A = y\), then express \(\cos A\) and \(\tan A\) in terms of y.
rows.solution:
For an acute angle A, \(\cos A = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A} = \sqrt{1 - y^2}\).

\(\tan A = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{1 - y^2}}\).

rows.stem: AD and PS are medians of triangles ABC and PQR respectively such that \(\Delta ABD \sim \Delta PQS\). Prove that \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\).
rows.solution:
\(\Delta ABD \sim \Delta PQS\), so \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BD}{QS}\) and \(\angle B = \angle Q\).

AD and PS are medians, so \(BC = 2BD\) and \(QR = 2QS\). Hence \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{2BD}{2QS} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\).

In triangles ABC and PQR, \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\) and the included angles \(\angle B = \angle Q\), so \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\) (SAS similarity).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem:
While shuffling a pack of 52 cards, one card was accidently dropped. Find the probability that the dropped card

(i) is not a face card.

(ii) is a black king.
rows.solution:
The dropped card is equally likely to be any of the 52.

(i) There are 12 face cards, so \(P(\text{not a face card}) = \dfrac{40}{52} = \dfrac{10}{13}\).

(ii) There are 2 black kings, so \(P(\text{black king}) = \dfrac{2}{52} = \dfrac{1}{26}\).

rows.stem:
State true or false for each of the following statements and justify in each case :

(i) \(2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 + 7\) is a composite number.

(ii) \(2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 + 1\) is a composite number.
rows.solution:
(i) True. \(2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 + 7 = 7(2 \times 3 \times 5 + 1) = 7 \times 31 = 217\). It has factors other than 1 and itself, so it is composite.

(ii) False. \(2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 + 1 = 211\). No prime up to \(\sqrt{211} \approx 14.5\) (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13) divides 211, so 211 is prime: it has only the two factors 1 and 211.

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: Obtain the zeroes of the polynomial \(7x^2 + 18x - 9\). Hence, write a polynomial each of whose zeroes is twice the zeroes of given polynomial.
rows.solution:
\(7x^2 + 18x - 9 = 7x^2 + 21x - 3x - 9 = 7x(x + 3) - 3(x + 3) = (7x - 3)(x + 3)\).

The zeroes are \(-3\) and \(\dfrac{3}{7}\).

Twice each zero: \(-6\) and \(\dfrac{6}{7}\).

Sum \(= -6 + \dfrac{6}{7} = -\dfrac{36}{7}\); product \(= -6 \times \dfrac{6}{7} = -\dfrac{36}{7}\).

The polynomial is \(x^2 + \dfrac{36}{7}x - \dfrac{36}{7}\), or \(7x^2 + 36x - 36\) (any non-zero multiple of it).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem:
Solve the following system of equations graphically :

\(2x - y - 2 = 0\)

\(-4x + y + 4 = 0\)

Also, find the absolute difference between the ordinates of the points where given lines cut y – axis.
rows.solution:
Points on \(2x - y - 2 = 0\) (that is, \(y = 2x - 2\)):

| \(x\) | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | \(-2\) | 0 | 2 |

Points on \(-4x + y + 4 = 0\) (that is, \(y = 4x - 4\)):

| \(x\) | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | \(-4\) | 0 | 4 |

Plot both sets of points and draw the two lines. They meet at \((1, 0)\), so the solution is \(x = 1\), \(y = 0\).

The lines cut the y-axis at \((0, -2)\) and \((0, -4)\). The absolute difference of the ordinates is \(|-2 - (-4)| = 2\).

rows.stem: Find a relation between x and y such that \(P(x, y)\) is equidistant from the points \(A(3, 5)\) and \(B(7, 1)\). Hence, write the coordinates of the points on x-axis and y-axis which are equidistant from points A and B.

Prove the following trigonometric identity :

\(\dfrac{1 + \operatorname{cosec} A}{\operatorname{cosec} A} = \dfrac{\cos^2 A}{1 - \sin A}\)
rows.solution:
LHS \(= \dfrac{1 + \frac{1}{\sin A}}{\frac{1}{\sin A}} = \sin A + 1\).

\(= \dfrac{(1 + \sin A)(1 - \sin A)}{1 - \sin A} = \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 A}{1 - \sin A} = \dfrac{\cos^2 A}{1 - \sin A} =\) RHS.

rows.stem: Let \(2A + B\) and \(A + 2B\) be acute angles such that \(\sin(2A + B) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\tan(A + 2B) = 1\). Find the value of \(\cot(4A - 7B)\).
rows.solution:
\(\sin(2A + B) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) with \(2A + B\) acute gives \(2A + B = 60^\circ\) ... (1)

\(\tan(A + 2B) = 1\) with \(A + 2B\) acute gives \(A + 2B = 45^\circ\) ... (2)

From (1), \(B = 60^\circ - 2A\). Substituting in (2): \(A + 120^\circ - 4A = 45^\circ\), so \(A = 25^\circ\) and \(B = 10^\circ\).

\(\cot(4A - 7B) = \cot(100^\circ - 70^\circ) = \cot 30^\circ = \sqrt{3}\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the adjoining figure, XY and \(X'Y'\) are parallel tangents to a circle with centre O. Another tangent AB touches the circle at C intersecting XY at A and \(X'Y'\) at B. Prove that AB subtends right angle at the centre of the circle; or \(\angle AOB = 90^\circ\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with centre O, parallel tangents XY and X'Y' touching at P and Q, and tangent AB touching at C with OA, OB joined; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Let XY touch the circle at P and \(X'Y'\) at Q. Join OC.

In triangles POA and COA: \(OP = OC\) (radii), \(AP = AC\) (tangents from A), and OA is common. So \(\Delta POA \cong \Delta COA\) (SSS), and \(\angle POA = \angle COA\).

Similarly \(\Delta QOB \cong \Delta COB\), and \(\angle QOB = \angle COB\).

The tangents at P and Q are parallel, so P, O, Q lie on a diameter and \(\angle POA + \angle COA + \angle COB + \angle QOB = 180^\circ\).

So \(2(\angle COA + \angle COB) = 180^\circ\), and \(\angle AOB = \angle COA + \angle COB = 90^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: A 2-digit number is seven times the sum of its digits and two (2) more than 5 times the product of its digits. Find the number.
rows.solution:
Let the units digit be x and the tens digit y. The number is \(10y + x\).

Seven times the sum of the digits: \(10y + x = 7(x + y)\), so \(3y = 6x\) and \(y = 2x\) ... (1)

Two more than 5 times the product: \(10y + x = 5xy + 2\) ... (2)

Substituting (1) in (2): \(20x + x = 10x^2 + 2\), so \(10x^2 - 21x + 2 = 0\) and \((x - 2)(10x - 1) = 0\).

A digit is a whole number, so \(x = 2\) and \(y = 4\). The number is 42.

(Check: \(7 \times (4 + 2) = 42\) and \(5 \times 4 \times 2 + 2 = 42\).)

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: Find the value(s) of p for which the quadratic equation given as \((p + 4)x^2 - (p + 1)x + 1 = 0\) has real and equal roots. Also, find the roots of the equation(s) so obtained.
rows.solution:
Real and equal roots need the discriminant to be zero:

\([-(p + 1)]^2 - 4(p + 4)(1) = 0\), so \(p^2 + 2p + 1 - 4p - 16 = 0\), that is \(p^2 - 2p - 15 = 0\).

\((p - 5)(p + 3) = 0\), so \(p = 5\) or \(p = -3\).

For \(p = 5\): \(9x^2 - 6x + 1 = 0\), that is \((3x - 1)^2 = 0\), and the roots are \(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\).

For \(p = -3\): \(x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0\), that is \((x + 1)^2 = 0\), and the roots are \(-1, -1\).

rows.stem:
If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides in distinct points then it divides the two sides in the same ratio. Prove it.

Also, state the converse of the above statement.
rows.solution:
Theorem (Basic Proportionality Theorem). Given: in triangle ABC, a line parallel to BC meets AB at D and AC at E. To prove: \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Construction: join BE and CD, and draw \(DM \perp AC\) and \(EN \perp AB\).

Proof: \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AD \cdot EN}{\frac{1}{2} DB \cdot EN} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}\), and \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(DEC)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AE \cdot DM}{\frac{1}{2} EC \cdot DM} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Triangles BDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so \(\text{ar}(BDE) = \text{ar}(DEC)\). Hence \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Converse: if a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: From one of the faces of a solid wooden cube of side 14 cm, maximum number of hemispheres of diameter 1.4 cm are scooped out. Find the total number of hemispheres that can be scooped out. Also, find the total surface area of the remaining solid.
rows.solution:
Along each 14 cm edge of the face, \(\dfrac{14}{1.4} = 10\) hemispheres of diameter 1.4 cm fit, so \(10 \times 10 = 100\) hemispheres can be scooped out.

Each removes a circle of radius 0.7 cm from the face and adds a curved surface of \(2\pi r^2\):

TSA \(= 6 \times 14^2 + 100 \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.7^2 - 100 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.7^2\)

\(= 1176 + 100 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.49 = 1176 + 154 = 1330\) cm\(^2\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: From a solid cylinder of height 24 cm and radius 5 cm, two cones of height 12 cm and radius 5 cm are hollowed out. Find the volume and surface area of the remaining solid.
rows.solution:
Each cone has \(r = 5\) cm and \(h = 12\) cm, hollowed from each end of the cylinder (\(r = 5\), \(h = 24\)).

Volume \(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 5^2 \times 24 - 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 5^2 \times 12 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 25 \times (24 - 8) = \dfrac{8800}{7}\) cm\(^3\), about 1257.14 cm\(^3\).

Slant height \(l = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13\) cm.

Both flat ends are removed, leaving the curved surface of the cylinder and the curved surfaces of the two cones:

Surface area \(= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 5 \times 24 + 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 5 \times 13 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 370 = \dfrac{8140}{7}\) cm\(^2\), about 1162.86 cm\(^2\).

Find the length of wire needed to fence the entire land.
rows.context:
A farmer has a circular piece of land. He wishes to construct his house in the form of largest possible square within the land as shown below.

The radius of circular piece of land is 35 m.

Based on given information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circular land with the largest square (the house plan) inscribed in it; the passage states the radius and that the square is the largest possible. The house drawing on the left is decorative. Page idx 18.
rows.solution: The fence is the circumference of the land: \(2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220\) m.

rows.stem: Find the length of each side of the square land on which house will be constructed.
rows.context:
A farmer has a circular piece of land. He wishes to construct his house in the form of largest possible square within the land as shown below.

The radius of circular piece of land is 35 m.

Based on given information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the square inscribed in the circular land; the passage states it is the largest possible square. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The largest square inside the circle has the diameter, 70 m, as its diagonal.

Side \(= \dfrac{70}{\sqrt{2}} = 35\sqrt{2}\) m.

rows.stem: The farmer wishes to grow grass on the shaded region around the house. Find the cost of growing the grass at the rate of ₹ 50 per square metre.
rows.context:
A farmer has a circular piece of land. He wishes to construct his house in the form of largest possible square within the land as shown below.

The radius of circular piece of land is 35 m.

Based on given information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - 'the shaded region around the house' is defined only by the drawing, which shades just TWO of the four segments (above and below the square, not the left and right ones); the scheme's 700 square metres is those two segments. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The shaded region is the two segments above and below the square. Each is cut off by a side of the square, which subtends \(90^\circ\) at the centre.

Area \(= 2\left[\dfrac{90}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 35 \times 35\right] = 2(962.5 - 612.5) = 700\) m\(^2\).

Cost \(= 700 \times 50\) = ₹35000.

rows.stem: Find the ratio of area of land on which house is built to remaining area of circular piece of land.
rows.context:
A farmer has a circular piece of land. He wishes to construct his house in the form of largest possible square within the land as shown below.

The radius of circular piece of land is 35 m.

Based on given information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Area of the square \(= (35\sqrt{2})^2 = 2450\) m\(^2\). Area of the circle \(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35^2 = 3850\) m\(^2\).

Remaining area \(= 3850 - 2450 = 1400\) m\(^2\).

Ratio \(= \dfrac{2450}{1400} = \dfrac{7}{4}\), that is \(7 : 4\).

rows.stem: How many triangles will be there in bottom most row ?
rows.context:
In an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm, equilateral triangles of side 1 cm are formed as shown in the figure below, such that there is one triangle in the first row, three triangles in the second row, five triangles in the third row and so on.

Based on given information, answer the following questions using Arithmetic Progression.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the triangle tiled with unit triangles, rows labelled 1st, 2nd, 3rd down to 10th Row; the passage gives the 1, 3, 5 pattern and the 10 cm side (so 10 rows). Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The triangle of side 10 cm has 10 rows, and the numbers of triangles in the rows form the AP 1, 3, 5, ..., with \(a = 1\) and \(d = 2\).

Bottom row: \(a_{10} = 1 + 9 \times 2 = 19\).

rows.stem: How many triangles will be there in fourth row from the bottom ?

Based on given information, answer the following questions using Arithmetic Progression.
rows.solution: The fourth row from the bottom is the 7th row: \(a_7 = 1 + 6 \times 2 = 13\).

rows.stem: How many more number of triangles are there from \(5^{\text{th}}\) row to \(10^{\text{th}}\) row than in first 4 rows ? Show working.
rows.context:
In an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm, equilateral triangles of side 1 cm are formed as shown in the figure below, such that there is one triangle in the first row, three triangles in the second row, five triangles in the third row and so on.

Based on given information, answer the following questions using Arithmetic Progression.
rows.solution:
Rows 5 to 10: \(S_{10} - S_4 = \dfrac{10}{2}[2 + 9 \times 2] - \dfrac{4}{2}[2 + 3 \times 2] = 100 - 16 = 84\).

First 4 rows: \(S_4 = 16\).

There are \(84 - 16 = 68\) more triangles in rows 5 to 10.

rows.stem: Find the angle at which stairs are inclined to reach the door sill 15 feet high above the ground.
rows.context:
Passenger boarding stairs, sometimes referred to as boarding ramps, stair cars or aircraft steps, provide a mobile means to travel between the aircraft doors and the ground. Larger aircraft have door sills 5 to 20 feet (1 foot = 30 cm) high. Stairs facilitate safe boarding and de-boarding.

An aircraft has a door sill at a height of 15 feet above the ground. A stair car is placed at a horizontal distance of 15 feet from the plane.

Based on given information, answer the questions given in part (i) and (ii).
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a photograph of a passenger on boarding stairs and a line drawing of a stair car labelled STAIRS; every number is in the passage. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
The stairs, the plane's side and the ground form a right triangle with height 15 feet and base 15 feet. Let the stairs make angle \(\theta\) with the ground.

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{15}{15} = 1\), so \(\theta = 45^\circ\).

rows.stem: Find the length of stairs used to reach the door sill.
rows.context:
Passenger boarding stairs, sometimes referred to as boarding ramps, stair cars or aircraft steps, provide a mobile means to travel between the aircraft doors and the ground. Larger aircraft have door sills 5 to 20 feet (1 foot = 30 cm) high. Stairs facilitate safe boarding and de-boarding.

An aircraft has a door sill at a height of 15 feet above the ground. A stair car is placed at a horizontal distance of 15 feet from the plane.

Based on given information, answer the questions given in part (i) and (ii).
rows.solution: \(\dfrac{15}{l} = \sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(l = 15\sqrt{2}\) feet, about 21.21 feet.

rows.stem: If the 20 feet long stairs is inclined at an angle of \(60^\circ\) to reach the door sill, then find the height of the door sill above the ground. (use \(\sqrt{3} = 1.732\))
rows.context:
Passenger boarding stairs, sometimes referred to as boarding ramps, stair cars or aircraft steps, provide a mobile means to travel between the aircraft doors and the ground. Larger aircraft have door sills 5 to 20 feet (1 foot = 30 cm) high. Stairs facilitate safe boarding and de-boarding.

An aircraft has a door sill at a height of 15 feet above the ground. A stair car is placed at a horizontal distance of 15 feet from the plane.

Based on given information, answer the questions given in part (i) and (ii).
rows.solution: \(\dfrac{h}{20} = \sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(h = 10\sqrt{3} = 10 \times 1.732 = 17.32\) feet.

rows.stem: What should be the shortest possible length of stairs to reach the door sill of the plane 20 feet above the ground, if the angle of elevation cannot exceed \(30^\circ\) ? Also, find the horizontal distance of base of stair car from the plane.
rows.context:
Passenger boarding stairs, sometimes referred to as boarding ramps, stair cars or aircraft steps, provide a mobile means to travel between the aircraft doors and the ground. Larger aircraft have door sills 5 to 20 feet (1 foot = 30 cm) high. Stairs facilitate safe boarding and de-boarding.

An aircraft has a door sill at a height of 15 feet above the ground. A stair car is placed at a horizontal distance of 15 feet from the plane.

Based on given information, answer the questions given in part (i) and (ii).
rows.solution:
The steepest allowed angle, \(30^\circ\), gives the shortest stairs.

\(\dfrac{20}{l} = \sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(l = 40\) feet.

\(\dfrac{20}{x} = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so the horizontal distance is \(x = 20\sqrt{3}\) feet, about 34.64 feet.
